scenes.narration: Twenty-two point six percent. That is how much the price of car insurance in America rose in a single year, by April twenty twenty-four. By our reading of government data, the biggest jump since nineteen seventy-six.

Over five years, car insurance prices rose almost fifty percent. Prices in general rose about twenty-three percent. And here is the twist. This year, for the first time in a long time, they have started to fall.
So what made car insurance so expensive, and who ended up making money from it?
By the end of this video, you will know the four forces behind your premium. The cars, the crashes, the courts, and the insurers' own books.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Start with what drivers actually pay. According to the National Association of Insurance Commissioners, the average American household spent one thousand four hundred and thirty-one dollars on auto insurance in twenty twenty-four, up almost twelve percent in a single year. In twenty twenty, it was about one thousand and forty-eight. By our calculation, that is a rise of about thirty-seven percent in four years.

Where you live matters. The most expensive state in twenty twenty-four was Florida, at about two thousand and eighteen dollars a year, followed by New York and Louisiana. The cheapest was North Dakota, at about nine hundred and seven. The regulators themselves warn that state comparisons should be treated with caution, because drivers buy very different coverage.

The government's price index tells the same story. By our calculation, car insurance prices rose about forty-nine percent in the five years to September twenty twenty-six. Over the same period, the price of new cars rose about twelve percent. Insurance outran the very thing it insures.

And people reacted. The insurance commissioners note that as prices rise, the amount of insurance people buy goes down. Drivers drop coverage, or raise their deductibles. Paying less today, but risking far more if they crash.

Let me draw what is inside a premium. A slice to repair or replace cars. A slice for people injured in crashes. A slice for lawyers and claims handling. A slice for the insurer's costs and profit. When any slice grows, the whole premium grows.

scenes.narration: The first slice to explode was the cost of fixing the car itself.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: During the pandemic, car factories ran short of chips, and used car prices shot up. The insurance commissioners report that used vehicle prices rose thirty-six percent between twenty nineteen and twenty twenty-three. When a car is totaled, the insurer pays what it is worth. Suddenly every totaled car cost much more.
Repairs climbed too, and kept climbing. By our calculation, the price of car maintenance and repair rose about forty-six percent in five years. Parts, paint and labor all became more expensive.

Modern cars are also harder to fix. Cameras and radar sit in bumpers, mirrors and windshields. The Highway Loss Data Institute, which is funded by insurers, found that for otherwise identical cars, those with driver assistance features cost about ten percent more per collision claim. The sensors are expensive, and often need calibration after a repair.

But there is a twist. The same technology prevents crashes. Cars with those features had about ten percent fewer collision claims, and almost forty percent fewer claims for damage to other people's property. A more expensive repair, but fewer of them.

Let me draw a modern bumper. On the outside, plastic and paint. Inside, a radar unit, sensors, wiring, and a camera behind the windshield. A small bump that once meant a cheap fix can now mean replacing and recalibrating electronics.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: Then there were the crashes themselves. And they got worse at the worst possible moment.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: In twenty twenty, roads emptied during lockdowns, but the crashes that did happen were deadlier. According to federal crash data compiled by the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, road deaths rose from about thirty-six thousand in twenty nineteen to forty-three thousand two hundred and thirty in twenty twenty-one. The death rate per mile driven jumped from one point one one to one point three eight.
Speed played a big part. In twenty twenty-four, speeding was a factor in twenty-nine percent of crash deaths. Faster crashes mean more injuries, more hospital bills, and bigger claims.
Since then, the roads have become somewhat safer again. Deaths fell to about thirty-nine thousand two hundred in twenty twenty-four. But that is still more than before the pandemic.

And not everyone on the road is paying. The Insurance Research Council, an industry-funded group, estimates that about one in seven drivers, fifteen point four percent, were uninsured in twenty twenty-three. When they cause a crash, the cost often lands on the insured driver's own policy.

Let me draw the death rate. Here is twenty nineteen, steady. Here is twenty twenty and twenty twenty-one, a sharp climb even as people drove less. Then a slow decline that has not returned to where it started. Insurers price for that whole curve.

scenes.narration: After the crash comes the claim. And in some states, the claim goes to court.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: The insurance commissioners' data show the price of legal services rising about twenty-one percent from twenty nineteen to twenty twenty-three, more than double the rise in medical care. The insurance industry blames what it calls legal system abuse. Its own study claims that, together with inflation, it added tens of billions of dollars to personal auto losses over ten years. That is the industry's own framing, not a neutral measurement.

Florida, the most expensive state, changed its laws in March twenty twenty-three. It repealed one-way attorney fees and cut the time to file a negligence lawsuit from four years to two years. Three years later, the state says loss ratios for car damage fell from one hundred and twelve percent in twenty twenty-two to under fifty percent in twenty twenty-five, and its biggest insurers are signaling rate cuts of about eight percent for twenty twenty-six.

States also decide how you can be priced. In California, rates are driven mainly by three mandatory factors, your safety record, the miles you drive, and your years of experience. Elsewhere, the commissioners say about ninety-five percent of auto insurers use credit-based insurance scores where they are allowed. Hawaii and Massachusetts bar rates based on credit.

Let me draw two drivers with the same car and the same clean record. One lives in a state that allows credit scores, the other does not. Same road, same risk on paper, different price. Your premium depends as much on the rules of your state as on how you drive.

scenes.narration: Which brings us to the companies in the middle. Were they the victims of this storm, or the winners?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: At first, they were losing. Insurers measure their business with the combined ratio, losses plus expenses as a share of premiums. Above one hundred means losing money on the policies. Allstate's auto combined ratio was one hundred and ten in twenty twenty-two. The company reported a net loss of one point three nine billion dollars that year.

So they raised prices, hard. Progressive says it raised personal auto rates by about thirteen percent in twenty twenty-two, and about nineteen percent in twenty twenty-three. Allstate took rate increases of almost eighteen percent for its main brand in fifty-five locations in twenty twenty-three.

Then the books flipped. By twenty twenty-five, Allstate's auto combined ratio was eighty-five, and its net income was ten point one seven billion dollars, partly from selling businesses. Progressive's net income went from seven hundred and twenty-two million dollars in twenty twenty-two to eleven point three billion dollars in twenty twenty-five.

In Florida, profits grew so large that a state law kicked in. Progressive recorded one point two two billion dollars of credits to policyholders, because its Florida auto profits exceeded the legal limit. And this year, Progressive reports that its average personal auto premium per policy is falling.

Let me draw the cycle. Costs rise faster than prices, and insurers lose money. Insurers raise prices, sharply. Costs cool down, but prices are already high, and profits soar. Then competition and regulators push prices back down. Drivers live through the expensive part of every turn.

So why did your car insurance get so expensive? More expensive cars and repairs, deadlier crashes, rising legal and medical costs, and insurers who raised prices fast to make up for their losses. Prices are finally easing. But they remain far above where they were before the pandemic, and the next turn of the cycle is never far away.
